name: James
interpretive_note: This entry's reference list touches an identification question Scripture does not fully resolve. Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3 name James as a brother of Jesus, and James 1:1 and Jude 1:1 are traditionally understood as this same James (the Lord's brother) and his brother Jude. But Matthew 27:56, Mark 15:40, Mark 16:1, and Luke 24:10 name a "Mary the mother of James" among the women at the cross and empty tomb -- most interpreters identify this James as James the son of Alphaeus, a different man among the Twelve, since none of these texts call this Mary "the mother of Jesus." This entry follows the majority reading (James, the Lord's brother) rather than treating the two as certainly the same person.
source_summary: One of Jesus' half-brothers, who did not believe in Him during His ministry but saw the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:7) and became a leader of the Jerusalem church -- "the Lord's brother" of Galatians 1:19, who spoke at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15) and is traditionally identified as the author of the epistle of James.
family_friendly_summary: James was one of Jesus' younger half-brothers, growing up in the same home in Nazareth. While Jesus was teaching and healing, His brothers -- including James -- didn't yet believe in Him. But after Jesus rose from the dead, He appeared to James, and everything changed. James became a leader of the church in Jerusalem. When the first Christians argued over whether believers who weren't Jewish had to be circumcised and keep all of Moses' law, James helped the church decide not to put that heavy load on them. He is also known for the New Testament letter that bears his name, full of practical wisdom about living out real faith -- famous for saying that faith without action is dead.
adult_story: James grew up in Nazareth as one of Jesus' younger half-brothers, the son of Mary, named alongside Joseph, Simon, and Judas when Jesus' hometown neighbors wondered how a carpenter's son could teach with such authority (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3). During Jesus' ministry His brothers did not believe in Him (John 7:5). That changed after the resurrection: Paul records that the risen Christ appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7). James became a recognized leader of the Jerusalem church. When Peter escaped from Herod's prison, he asked that word be sent to James (Acts 12:17). Paul, visiting Jerusalem after his conversion, met "James, the Lord's brother" (Galatians 1:19), and later named him with Peter and John as the church's pillars (Galatians 2:9). At the Jerusalem council James summed up the debate: God was calling a people for His name from among the Gentiles, so the church should not trouble Gentile believers who were turning to God, asking only that they keep away from idols, sexual immorality, and blood (Acts 15:13-21). Years later Paul reported his missionary work to James and all the elders (Acts 21:18). James is traditionally identified as the author of the letter bearing his name, which opens simply "James, a bond-servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" (James 1:1) and insists that genuine faith shows itself in works; Jude calls himself "brother of James" (Jude 1:1). His life traces one of the New Testament's clearest arcs from unbelief to faithful service.
devotionals: James doubted his own brother Jesus during his earthly ministry. Jesus patiently turned him into a faithful servant — may he turn us too.
The risen Jesus appeared to James, the brother who had grown up beside him and still not believed. God can turn even a lifelong doubter into a pillar of the church.
James wrote that faith without works is dead. May our trust in Jesus show up in what we actually do.
